newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France may win euro deal in time for summit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France may win euro deal in time for summit.

text.p: France's new Socialist government appeared on Wednesday to be on the way to securing a deal adding pledges to promote economic growth and jobs to a European Union budget discipline pact in time for next week's Amsterdam summit.

European Commission President Jacques Santer said he expected the summit next Monday and Tuesday to agree on the so-called stability pact, limiting the deficits of countries that join a single European currency due to be launched in 1999.

Germany, Europe's chief stickler for fiscal discipline, signalled an apparent willingness to accommodate some French concerns, saying it would accept a long-resisted jobs chapter in the revised European union treaty to be adopted in Amsterdam.

"We do not want any unaccountable, unfinanceable or expensive spending programmes. An improved coordination of national measures on European level can take us further. Under this sign, the German government will agree to a jobs chapter," Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told parliament in Bonn.

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, the summit host, was to discuss proposals for closer economic policy coordination with Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Wednesday before Santer meets French leaders on Thursday and Kohl and Kinkel visit France on Friday.

Officials said the key was to find wording that would be acceptable to France without causing major problems for Germany's weakened coalition government, which insists on strict respect for the criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU).

The new French government requested time on Monday to study the pact, which the Socialists had criticised in last month's election campaign, and said it wanted balancing commitments to coordinate EU economic policies to promote employment.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac, while supporting the government's demand for a greater emphasis on growth and jobs, said after meeting Kok on Tuesday he hoped an enhanced pact could be concluded in Amsterdam.
Government spokesman Catherine Trautmann said there was no divergence on European policy between Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who requested the initial delay, said after a cabinet meeting: "If we can move forward quickly, it is obviously better. No one wants to drag things out for the sake of it.
"The question is to know how we can obtain the balance we are seeking," he said.
Speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Santer urged EU states not to jeopardise plans to approve wide-ranging reforms of the union's institutions next week.
"If we can make improvements, let's do that, but let's not jeopardise the project by last minute special pleading which may undermine the balance we have arrived at," Santer said.
EU leaders are due to ratify the pact at the same time as they approved internal EU reforms designed to prepare the 15-member bloc for its ambitious expansion eastward.

The Commission is working to find a way to meet France's concerns, and sources said Santer would offer a compromise attaching resolutions on coordinating economic and employment policy to the stability pact when he visits Paris on Thursday.
Since employment is also an issue in the EU treaty talks, some officials have voiced concern that the advent of the new government might prevent the treaty's completion in Amsterdam.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU presidency, told the EU assembly he was confident the French would find a solution to allow the stability pact to be approved at Amsterdam, "but it's not in the bag yet".
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union warned France not to seek a watering down of the EMU criteria.

The warning comes a week after Waigel had to step in to quell rumours that the CSU, a core part of the German coalition government, would push for an outright delay of EMU following the election of the Socialists in France.
